figure.name: Warren Buffett
figure.era: Berkshire Hathaway, value investing, and philanthropy (1950-present)
figure.role: Investor, Berkshire Hathaway leader, billionaire philanthropist, and example of patient capital, insurance float, corporate ownership, and shareholder capitalism.
figure.hook: Buffett = investing, Berkshire Hathaway, compounding, insurance float, and philanthropy.
whyHere: Buffett belongs here because American capitalism is not only factories, oil, banks, and tech. It is also ownership: buying pieces of companies and letting compounding do political and economic work over time.
He matters because he makes capitalism look calmer than the robber-baron or platform-power versions, while still concentrating enormous wealth and corporate influence.
figure.cleanIdea: Investment capitalism can look patient and disciplined, but it still raises questions about ownership, compounding, corporate control, taxes, and philanthropy. Buffett is useful because he makes capitalism look less like conquest and more like allocation: who owns, who waits, who compounds, and who gets a say.

ideas.title: Investment Capital
ideas.plainDefinition: Investment capital is money used to buy ownership claims, finance companies, hold assets, earn returns, and compound wealth over time.
ideas.context: In the Buffett path, investment capital is patient ownership rather than direct factory command or platform control.
ideas.whyMatters: Investment capital matters because ownership itself can become a governing force in the economy. A person does not have to run a factory floor or hold office to influence corporate priorities; capital allocation can steer what gets built, bought, preserved, or shut down.

sources.title: Warren Buffett / Wikipedia
sources.note: Source lead for investment career and Berkshire pathway; supports the move from personal investor to corporate ownership lesson.

ideas.title: Shareholder Power
ideas.plainDefinition: Shareholder power is influence over companies through ownership, voting rights, boards, capital allocation, and market pressure.
ideas.context: In the Buffett path, shareholder power shows how capitalism can govern through ownership without direct political office.
ideas.whyMatters: Shareholder power matters because companies answer to ownership, and ownership is not evenly distributed. This is the quieter side of capitalist control: votes, boards, expectations, buybacks, dividends, and long-term ownership discipline.

sources.title: Berkshire Hathaway / Wikipedia
sources.note: Source lead for Berkshire structure and shareholder framing; supports the claim that ownership can act as economic governance.

ideas.title: Giving Pledge
ideas.plainDefinition: The Giving Pledge is a billionaire philanthropy campaign asking wealthy people to commit most of their wealth to charitable causes.
ideas.context: In the Buffett path, the Giving Pledge links investment wealth to private philanthropy and public-good claims.
ideas.whyMatters: The Giving Pledge matters because philanthropy may do real good while still leaving democratic questions about wealth, taxation, and public priorities. The honest lesson keeps both truths visible: giving can help people, and giant private fortunes still shape public life outside ordinary democratic channels.
